Talabis, This refers to your letter dated March 15, 2017, requesting for a legal opinion on the validity of Ordinance No. 12-01, Series of 2016 of Barangay Ayala Alabang, Muntinlupa City, entitled: "An Ordinance Authorizing the Expropriation of a Parcel of Land in Filinvest Alabang for a Road Right of Way." The factual antecedents are heretofore quoted from your letter, viz: "On December 7, 2016/ Barangay Ayala Alabang in Muntinlupa City issued Brgy. Ordinance No. 12-01, Series of 2016, entitled "An Ordinance Authorizing the Expropriation of a Parcel of Land in Filinvest Alabang for a Road Right of Way." This Ordinance authorizes the Punong Barangay to acquire through expropriation two adjoining lots inside Filinvest City, Alabang, Muntinlupa City, with a total area of 1,200 square meters: a) the entire parcel covered by Transfer Certificate of Title No. 014-2014000258 with an area of 970 square meters; and b) an undivided portion measuring 230 square meters in the parcel covered by TCT No. 014-2014000259. Both lands are co-owned by the Republic of the Philippines (26%) and Filinvest Alabang, Inc. (74%) under a Joint Venture Agreement (JVA). Both lots are located in Brgy. Alabang, a separate and distinct barangay, outside the territorial jurisdiction of Barangay Ayala Alabang. The expropriation is supposedly meant for the opening of an alternate gate to and from Ayala Alabang Village (AAV) along San Jose Street connecting to Filinvest City through the two mentioned lots. It is noted that the ordinance in question was approved by the Sangguniang Barangay of Ayala Alabang on December 7, 2016, and the same was already forwarded to the Sangguniang Panlungsod, City of Muntinlupa, on December 14, 2016, for review pursuant to Section 57 of Republic Act No. 71601. On the assumed premise that the expropriation ordinance was able to pass review, the same is therefore presumed valid unless judicially reprobated. It bears emphasis that duly approved ordinances are presumptively valid acts and thus enjoy the presumption of regularity on the part of the public officer concerned, unless declared otherwise by our courts of justice upon proper judicial action.2 Be that as it may, the Department could not help but state a fundamental rule in the exercise of governmental powers by the local government unit. The well-entrenched rule is that powers of the government are exercisable within its territorial definition. In a case, it was settled by the Supreme Court that the importance of drawing with precise strokes the territorial boundaries of a local unit of government cannot be overemphasized. The boundaries must be clear for they define the limits of the territorial jurisdiction of a local government unit. It can legitimately exercise povvers of government only within the limits of its territorial jurisdiction. Beyond this limits, its acts are ultra vires.3 With regard to the second query, the following pronouncements of the Supreme Court in the case of Vda. de Ouano, et al. v. Republic, et aL4find relevance: I The Local Government Code of 1991 - DILG Opinion No. 24 S. 2011, June 14, 2011 Mariano, Jr. vs. Commission on Elections, G.R. No. 118577, March 7, 1995 and Osmefia vs. Commission on Elections, G.R. no. 118627, March 7, 1995, 242 SCRA 211 233 Phil. 313 (1987) [Per J. Gutierrez, Jr., En Banc]. 2

"In esse xpropriation is forced private p -erty taking, the landowner being really without a ghost of a chance to defeat the case of the expropriating agency. In other words, in expropriation, the private owner is deprived of property against his will. Withal, the mandatory requirement of due process ought to be strictly followed, such that the state must show, at the minimum, a genuine need, an exacting public purpose to take private property, the purpose to be specifically alleged or least reasonably deducible from the complaint. Public use, as an eminent domain concept, has now acquired an expansive 'meaning to include any use that is of "usefulness, utility, or advantage, or what is productive of general benefit [of the public]. " If the genuine public necessity—the very reason or condition as it were— allowing, at the first instance, the expropriation of a private land ceases or disappears, then there is no more cogent point for the government's retention of the expropriated land. The same legal situation should hold if the government devotes the property to another public use very much different from the original or deviates from the declared purpose to benefit another private person. It has been said that the direct use by the state of its power to oblige landowners to renounce their productive possession to another citizen, who will use it predominantly for that citizen's own private gpin, is offensive to our laws. A condemnor should commit to use the property pursuant to the purpose stated in the petition for expropriation, failing which it should file another petition for the new purpose. If not, then it behooves the condemnor to return the said property to its private owner, if the latter so desires. The government cannot plausibly keep the property it expropriated in any manner it pleases and, in the process, dishonor the judgment of expropriation. This is not in keeping with the idea of fair play. It is the state that bears the burden of proving that the taking of private property is for a public purpose. If it fails in discharging this burden, it must return the property to the private owner, subject to whatever damages were incurred in the course of the taking." (emphasis supplied) Withal, based on the foregoing ratiocinations by the Supreme Court, it behooves this Department to refrain from rendering an opinion as regards 3
